opus-5.5.text:
I think the data wall is a real consideration, but I'm not sure it's as hard a wall as people sometimes make it sound. It's true that we've been scaling up pretraining by pulling in more and more of the internet, and at some point you run out of high-quality text. So you can't just keep turning the same crank forever.

But there are a few reasons I'm not too worried about it being a hard stop. First, there's still room to get more out of the data we have. You can train for multiple epochs, you can be smarter about filtering and mixing, and models are getting better at extracting signal from a given amount of data. Second, there's a lot of data in other modalities, like video, audio, and images, that hasn't been fully exploited, and it's plausible some of that transfers to general capabilities.

The bigger shift, though, is that more of the progress is going to come from things other than passively predicting internet text. Reinforcement learning, having models generate their own data, letting them attempt problems and get feedback on whether they succeeded. That kind of data is in some sense unlimited, because you can keep generating it, and it's also more targeted at the behaviors you care about, like reasoning through a hard problem or carrying out a long task. There are real research challenges there. You have to avoid the model just reinforcing its own mistakes, and you need good ways to verify or judge outputs. But I'd expect the field to adapt rather than stall.

So my overall view is that pretraining on raw text will probably see diminishing returns at some point, and the mix of where improvements come from will change. I'd be surprised if that turned into a wall that actually stops progress. It's more like the easy path gets harder, and people find other paths, which is what's happened at each previous stage.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot. The naive version of the data wall argument is: we've trained on most of the high-quality text on the internet, the amount of that text is roughly fixed, compute keeps growing, so at some point you're compute-rich and data-poor and the scaling curves bend. I think that's directionally right about pretraining in the narrow sense, but I don't think it's a wall for progress overall, for a few reasons.

First, we haven't actually exhausted data. People talk about "the internet" as a fixed quantity, but there's a lot of multimodal data, video, audio, that's barely been touched relative to text. There's also a lot of text that's not on the public web. And even on the web, the amount of useful signal depends on how good your filtering and curation is. We've found repeatedly that going from a mediocre dataset to a well-curated one is worth a lot of raw tokens.

Second, you can do multiple epochs. The old folk wisdom was you only pass over the data once, but the empirical work suggests you can go several epochs with pretty mild degradation. That buys you a few more doublings.

Third, and this is the one I think matters most, pretraining on natural text is not the only way to improve the model. Once a model is good enough to do useful things, you can start generating training signal from the model's own behavior. That's what RL is. If you have tasks where you can verify the answer, like code that has to pass tests, or math with a checkable solution, or agentic tasks where the environment tells you whether you succeeded, you can generate essentially unlimited experience. The model's own rollouts become the data. So the question shifts from "how much text exists" to "how many tasks can we build good reward signals for," and that's a much more open-ended frontier.

The honest caveat is that the RL route is harder. Pretraining is a very forgiving objective; you just predict the next token and everything works. With RL you have to worry about reward hacking, about the environments being representative of what you actually care about, about generalization from the narrow tasks you can verify to the fuzzy ones you can't. So I'd expect progress to feel less like the clean, predictable scaling of the past few years and more like engineering effort on environments and reward models. But I'd describe that as a change in what the bottleneck is, not as hitting a wall.

If you forced me to put a number on it, I'd say I'm fairly confident the pretraining data constraint will bite for the largest runs within the next couple of years, and fairly confident that won't translate into a plateau in capabilities, because the field already shifted its center of gravity toward post-training.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a real concern, but I’m uncertain about how hard a wall it is. There’s a finite amount of high-quality text on the internet, so you can’t count on getting more data indefinitely just by crawling more websites. But that’s different from saying we’re running out of ways to improve models.

One question is how much more we can learn from the data we already have. Humans seem to get quite a lot out of comparatively little experience, which suggests there’s room to improve learning efficiency. That doesn’t tell us how easy those improvements will be.

The other question is whether models can generate useful new experience through reinforcement learning. In domains where you can check an answer or observe whether an action worked, a model can try things and learn from the outcome. Code is a natural example: you can run it and see what happens. You’re getting a learning signal beyond simply imitating existing text.

The challenge is extending that to tasks where success is harder to evaluate. Generating more text by itself doesn’t necessarily give you more useful information. You need some way to distinguish improvements from mistakes.

So I’d take the constraint on pretraining data seriously. I’m less convinced that it implies a general ceiling on progress. A lot depends on how well we can turn computation and interaction into useful learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a real concern, but I wouldn’t interpret running out of new text on the internet as running out of ways to improve models. Those are different things.

One question is how much more we can get out of the data we already have. Seeing an example once doesn’t mean you’ve extracted everything useful from it. Better training methods might let us learn substantially more from the same corpus.

The other question is whether we can generate useful new experience. In domains like programming or math, a model can try something and get feedback about whether it worked. That gives you a way to improve that isn’t just imitating more human-written text. But generating text by itself isn’t enough—you need some way to distinguish good outputs from bad ones. Otherwise you can just reinforce your existing mistakes.

So I’m uncertain about how much of a bottleneck data will become. I’d expect it to change the mix of methods that drive progress, rather than necessarily bring progress to a stop.
